client: I just don't feel like doing anything anymore. We used to go hiking every weekend, and now even looking at our hiking gear in the closet makes me want to cry. Everyone keeps telling me I should "get back out there," but how am I supposed to enjoy things we loved doing together when they're not here anymore?
therapist: I hear how deeply painful this loss feels—your voice sounds both hurt and overwhelmed when you talk about the hiking gear. It makes sense that activities you shared would feel empty right now, and that pressure from others might add to the burden. Would it feel possible to explore what small step might honor your memories without feeling unbearable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate you acknowledging how hard this is, but I’m not sure what kind of small step would even help. Every time I think about doing something related to hiking, I just feel this heavy emptiness—like I’m forcing myself to pretend things are okay when they’re not. Even the idea of honoring memories feels overwhelming because it just reminds me of what I’ve lost.
therapist: Your voice sounds so drained when you describe that heavy emptiness—it’s clear this grief still weighs deeply on you, without needing to be rushed. Perhaps instead of pushing toward hiking, we could explore what feels manageable right now, even if it’s completely unrelated? This pain deserves space, not pressure to perform healing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you recognizing how heavy this feels—it’s like I’m carrying this grief everywhere, but I don’t know what to do with it. I guess the idea of doing something unrelated feels strange because everything seems connected to this loss somehow. Even small things feel overwhelming.
therapist: It sounds like this grief has woven itself into so many parts of your life—your voice carries a quiet heaviness when you talk about how even small things feel overwhelming. Let’s take a moment to sit with that together, without needing to fix it right now. Would it feel okay to explore how this grief shows up in those everyday moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I guess it does feel overwhelming a lot. Like yesterday I was at the grocery store and saw my mom’s favorite cereal, and suddenly I couldn’t even remember why I came there. It’s been months, but these little things still hit me out of nowhere. I don’t know if exploring it will help—sometimes I just want to push through it instead of dwelling on it, you know?
therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and tense when you describe these moments—it’s clear how much these unexpected reminders shake you, even when you’re trying to keep moving forward. It’s okay to feel torn between wanting to push through and needing to acknowledge the pain; both are valid responses to such a deep loss. Would it feel helpful to explore how to balance those two needs in a way that feels manageable for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate you acknowledging how I feel—it’s true, I’m constantly torn between pushing forward and feeling stuck in the grief. I want to move on, but it feels like every time I try, something triggers me, and I’m right back where I started. I’m not sure how to balance it—it feels like I’m failing at both, honestly.
therapist: I hear the frustration in your voice—it’s understandably exhausting to feel caught between moving forward and being pulled back by grief. It might help to reframe this not as failing at either, but as a natural ebb and flow of healing that doesn’t follow a straight line. Would it feel accurate to say that even when triggers bring you back, you’re carrying a bit more strength each time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about the ebb and flow, but it's hard to believe I'm actually getting stronger when every setback feels just as painful as the first time. Last night I dreamt about my dad again, and waking up felt like losing him all over again. Part of me wonders if this pain will ever really change, you know?
therapist: Your voice sounds both urgent and shaky when you describe that dream—it’s clear how deeply these waves of grief still pull at you, making progress feel impossible in those raw moments. What if we explored how this pain might not disappear, but could gradually take up less of your emotional energy over time? Even acknowledging that possibility takes courage when the hurt feels so fresh.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I don't know if I can believe that the pain will ever take up less space. When I wake up from those dreams about my mom, it feels like the grief is just as heavy as the day she died. Everyone keeps telling me time will help, but two years later it still hurts just as much.
therapist: Your voice sounds both fragile and hurried as you share this—it’s clear how deeply these dreams reopen that wound, and how exhausting it must feel to carry that same weight after two years. It’s okay if time hasn’t eased the pain in the way others expect—healing isn’t about forgetting, but finding ways to carry your mom’s memory without it overwhelming you. Would it feel possible to explore what small moments of comfort might look like amidst this grief?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I don't know... the idea of finding "small moments of comfort" just makes me feel guilty, like I'm trying to replace her or move on too fast. When I do have a good day, I end up feeling worse afterward because it's like I'm betraying her memory. 

I guess what scares me is that if I stop feeling this pain all the time, it'll mean I loved her less. The dreams are awful, but at least they keep her close, you know?
therapist: Your voice sounds so tender and hesitant as you share this—I can hear how deeply conflicted you feel between honoring your mom and allowing yourself moments of relief. That fear about the pain meaning love is completely understandable, and so human. What if we gently explored how carrying her memory could coexist with moments of peace, not as replacement, but as proof of how deeply she shaped your capacity to feel?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe that's possible, but it just feels... wrong somehow. Like if I'm not suffering, it means I didn't love her enough. The guilt creeps in every time I catch myself laughing or enjoying something. How could her absence hurt this much if I'm able to feel okay sometimes?
therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and strained as you share this—it’s clear how much this guilt weighs on you, especially when it interrupts moments of joy. What if we explored how your love for her isn’t measured by pain, but by the depth of your connection and the way she shaped who you are? Even in moments of laughter, she’s still very much a part of you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I want to believe that, but it's hard. Whenever I start to feel happy, this voice in my head says "How can you be happy when she's gone?" It's like I'm betraying her memory by not being sad all the time. The guilt just crashes over me like a wave.
therapist: I hear both the struggle and the quiet resignation in your voice as you describe that inner critic—it’s as if allowing any happiness feels like letting go of her, when really it’s proof of how deeply she lives on in you. That guilt must feel so heavy in those moments—would it be okay to explore how your mom might have wanted you to experience joy, too, as part of honoring her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech
